title: Paediatric Neurological Disorders
subject: Paediatrics
summary: A practical guide for ward rounds in low‑resource settings, focusing on common infections, metabolic causes, and red‑flag signs that require urgent referral. It blends history, exam, and pragmatic investigations.

sections.p: Neurological disorders in children encompass any abnormality of the nervous system that affects structure or function, from seizures to developmental delay. Diagnosis starts with a focused history, bedside exam, and targeted investigations.
b: History of onset, triggers, family history
Cranial nerve exam, motor strength, tone, reflexes

t.b: Normal or mild anaemia – not cause of seizures
Low sodium <130 mmol/L or low potassium <3.5 mmol/L
High WCC >1000/µL or low glucose <2.5 mmol/L

sections.p: Use the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) for altered consciousness and the Modified Rankin Scale for functional outcome. Seizure severity is staged by frequency and duration.

In East Africa, infections dominate: malaria, meningitis, HIV, and schistosomiasis. Metabolic causes include hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, and thiamine deficiency. Genetic disorders such as cerebral palsy and congenital infections (TORCH) are also common.
Presentations vary: seizures, altered consciousness, focal deficits, developmental delay, or chronic pain. Look for fever, neck stiffness, or signs of raised intracranial pressure.
Prioritise tests that are affordable and available. Use point‑of‑care devices where possible.
Urgent red flags include persistent vomiting, papilledema, focal seizures, or sudden loss of consciousness. Complications may be raised ICP, seizures, or death.
b: Severe hyponatraemia leading to cerebral oedema

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care. Avoid drugs that worsen the primary condition or are unavailable.
b: Monitor for complications: ICP, renal function

sections.p: Schedule regular neurodevelopmental assessments, immunisations, and malaria prophylaxis. Educate caregivers on recognising early seizure signs.
b: Counselling on safe sleep and head injury prevention

sections.p: Seizures can mimic febrile illness; developmental delay may be mistaken for cerebral palsy; raised ICP may be confused with dehydration.
Normal CSF glucose can occur in early meningitis; malaria antigen tests may be negative in low parasitaemia; thiamine levels are rarely measured.
b: Thiamine assay unavailable in most labs

faq.q: What is the first step if a child has a seizure in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Check airway, breathing, circulation; give oxygen if needed; start phenobarbital or phenytoin if seizures continue.

faq.q: How do you differentiate febrile seizures from meningitis?
faq.a: Look for neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness, and perform a lumbar puncture if any red flag is present.

faq.q: Why is thiamine given before glucose in suspected deficiency?
faq.a: Glucose can worsen neurological injury by driving glucose into cells while thiamine is needed for energy metabolism.

exam: A 6‑month‑old presents with seizures and fever. What is the next best investigation? — Check for meningitis: lumbar puncture if no contraindication; malaria test if endemic.
A child with HIV has new onset seizures. What is the most likely cause? — Opportunistic infection such as cryptococcal meningitis or PML; start empirical therapy.
A 4‑year‑old with chronic renal failure has tremors. What is the most common neurological disorder? — Guillain‑Barré syndrome is rare; the most common is peripheral neuropathy due to uremic toxins.
A child with a history of malaria now has papilledema. What complication should you suspect? — Cerebral malaria leading to raised intracranial pressure.
A 2‑year‑old with developmental delay is found to have normal head circumference. What is a likely diagnosis? — Cerebral palsy or spastic diplegia from prematurity.

A child presents with vomiting, headache, and seizures. Serum sodium is 125 mmol/L. What is the immediate treatment? — Rapid but controlled correction of hyponatraemia with hypertonic saline, monitoring for osmotic demyelination.
A 3‑year‑old with seizures is started on phenobarbital. What side effect should you monitor? — Hepatotoxicity and sedation; check liver function if available.
A child with suspected meningitis has a normal CSF glucose. What should you consider? — Early meningitis or partially treated infection; repeat LP if clinical suspicion remains high.
